extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, aspiring novelists, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing and composing novels: identifies core aspects (Story, People, Plot, Fantasy/Prophecy, Pattern and Rhythm) and gives practical evaluative criteria and illustrative examples from canonical authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse chronology / see literature beyond time
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must 'refuse to have anything to do with chronology' and 'see literature steadily and see it whole... beyond time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize novelists together irrespective of date/place; avoid treating works primarily as products of their historical moment. The critic who has not read widely should nevertheless try to cut off chronology and judge novels as if outside their immediate historical context. (Quoted guidance: T. S. Eliot's duties of the critic: preserve tradition when it exists and see literature beyond time — but Forster notes we may be unable to preserve tradition and so should at least attempt the second duty.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is the fundamental aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental aspect of the novel is its story-telling aspect: 'a story is a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a story qua story, its sole merit is 'making the audience want to know what happens next' and its sole fault is making the audience not want to know. The story is the 'backbone' of the novel — primitive and simple, yet indispensable. Evaluate whether the narrative sustains curiosity and forward motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include 'life by values' as well as 'life in time'
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily life comprises 'the life in time' and 'the life by values'; a good novel should include both rather than merely narrating chronological events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the novel transcends pure chronology by incorporating events measured by intensity or value (pinnacles of experience) so it does more than a mere sequence of 'and then...and then.' Devices to incorporate value-life will be discussed elsewhere; lack of this double allegiance leaves work shallow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-sequence is imperative — cannot abolish time entirely
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist cannot fully deny time within the fabric of a novel: even experimental manipulations of chronology must retain some time-sense or the work becomes unintelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devices that alter or play with temporal order (Emily Brontë, Sterne, Proust) are legitimate, but total abolition (Forster cites Gertrude Stein) tends to destroy intelligibility and value. When evaluating experimental fiction, check whether temporal play serves intelligibility and communicates values, rather than simply destroying sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense is the essential tool of the story-teller
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense — making the audience wonder 'what will happen next?' — is the primitive, effective instrument of the story-teller (illustrated by Scheherazade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the novelist's skill in sustaining curiosity: the tactical stopping of action, withholding of information, and creation of expectation. Even when other elements (description, morality, character) exist, the story-teller often relies principally on suspense to hold the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish story from plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A story (sequence of events) is not the same as a plot, which is 'an organism of a higher type.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate mere chronological narration with structural design. Expect plot-based evaluation to consider higher-order organization, causality, and thematic shaping beyond raw sequence; the story alone is the lower-level backbone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story often benefits from ragged ends and episodic digressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The story-teller may profit by 'ragged ends' — incidents and introductions that do not always tie causally into the main development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether apparent loose ends or episodic material serve the telling (maintain interest, provide texture) rather than harm the work. Forster uses Sir Walter Scott as example: digressions and seemingly irrelevant turns can still engage the primitive reader and serve the story-telling voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as a voice — oral/read-aloud quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The story has a vocal quality: it 'asks to be read out loud' and transforms readers into listeners; voice adds something beyond the written sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the oral/audible qualities of prose (cadence, directness, spoken rhythm) and whether the writing gains from being imagined or read aloud. Recognize that voice adds immediacy even if it is not equivalent to the author's personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting sentimentality dominate judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The final test of a novel involves our affection for it, but 'sentimentality...must not speak too loudly or too soon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of evaluations that rest primarily on personal liking without critical discrimination. Affection is a natural test, but critics should guard against sentimentality that clouds analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should reveal hidden inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the novelist's chief functions is to reveal the hidden or 'romanesque' side of human beings — their dreams, joys, sorrows and inner communings — beyond what history or external actions show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characters by how effectively they expose interiority and intentionality. Alain's point: fiction's method shows thought developing into action; the novelist can make characters more fully knowable than in life, and that deliberate exposure is a key criterion of fictional characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make fictional characters exact historical replicas
rubrics_metrics.description: If a character is exactly like a real historical person (e.g., Queen Victoria), the work becomes memoir or history rather than a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether characters are fictional creations shaped by the novelist's temperament rather than verbatim reproductions of real figures. Faithful depiction is different from replication; novels must create rather than merely record to avoid becoming documentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelistic persons are conditioned by the novelist's temperament and other novel aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are 'word-masses roughly describing himself' and their nature is conditioned by what the novelist guesses about others and about himself, and modified by the novel's other aspects (plot, pattern, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging characters, consider the author's temperament and how other aspects of the work (plot, tone, pattern) shape and limit character portrayal. Character must be appraised in context of the whole novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictional characters can be 'more definite' than real people
rubrics_metrics.description: People in novels can be understood completely by the reader if the novelist chooses; they may seem more definite than historical figures or friends because all relevant information is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use completeness of portrayal as a criterion: has the novelist intentionally exposed inner and outer life to produce a fully knowable figure, and does that clarity serve the work's aims?

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of space/place can elevate a novel beyond mere time-sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist's sense of space (the vast area of Russia in War and Peace) can create grandeur and sonority that the story alone does not produce; space can be the lord of a novel as much as time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the novel develops a convincing, expansive sense of place/space that accumulates weight and musical effect over the course of the book; this may counterbalance or complement the temporal narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelist's method distinguishes fiction from history: intentionality vs fatality
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas history is 'dominated by the notion of fatality' and external causes, the novel presents existence where 'everything is intentional' — passions, crimes, and miseries are rooted in human nature and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether actions and events in the novel flow from character intentions and inner motives rather than being presented as inevitable external forces; check that the method of thought-to-action development is coherent and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as literary material: the five main facts of human life
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster posits that the main facts of human life (birth, food, sleep, love, death) are the obvious raw material for characters; a novelist may choose to reproduce, exaggerate, minimize, or ignore these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing characterization, note how the novelist uses these elemental human facts — whether rendered realistically or transformed for artistic effect — and whether those choices suit the novel's aims.
